source: Mackworth (1977) Consistency in networks of relations
finding: Defines the CSP as variables, finite domains, unary and binary predicates, drawn as a network. Names three causes of thrashing in backtracking: node inconsistency (a value fails a unary predicate), arc inconsistency (a value has no partner in a neighbour), path inconsistency (a pair fits but no third value fits both).
numbers: Example network of Fig 1: 5 nodes, D1=D2={a,b,c}, D3=D4=D5={a,b}, P = strict lexicographic order; the backtrack tree repeats the same failure many times.
quote: The most obvious source of inefficiency and the easiest to prevent concerns the unary predicates.
limits: Theory paper; the example is a toy. Exponential cost of backtracking is asserted, not measured.
agent_relevance: O4 and S4: remove values that cannot appear in any solution before guessing. Each inconsistency maps to a cheap check the program can run on an agent's constraint list.

source: Mackworth (1977) AC-1, AC-2, AC-3 and PC algorithms
finding: AC-1 re-sweeps all arcs until nothing changes. AC-2 follows Waltz filtering and spreads outward from a newly added node. AC-3 queues only arcs that a deletion may have broken, and does not re-queue arcs already waiting. AC-2 is a special case of AC-3. The paper also gives a new path-consistency algorithm (PC-1, PC-2).
numbers: AC-1 worst case stated as O(a^2) in the number of arcs a. PC-2 needs only one pass over the initial (n^2+n^2-n)/2 paths if they are queued in PC-1 order.
limits: 1977 complexity claims were later corrected (see a04 and a09). No benchmark runs in the paper.
agent_relevance: The idea of queueing only what a change can affect fits an agent: after one edit to a plan, recheck only the constraints touching it.

source: Mackworth (1977) Waltz filtering, Montanari, applications
finding: Traces the history: Montanari (1974) gave the formal theory of path consistency; Waltz (1972, 1975) gave picture-junction filtering, the arc consistency special case. Applications named: Instant Insanity and cryptarithmetic (Gaschnig), n-queens, magic squares, map and scene interpretation. Waltz's results suggest time could be linear in picture complexity.
numbers: No new numbers. Linear time is credited to T junctions not passing constraints from stem to crossbar.
limits: Linearity is attributed to that decoupling, with 'no reason to expect' it in other domains.
agent_relevance: Propagation works best on decoupled sub-problems. Split a task into parts that do not interact before propagating.

source: Mackworth and Freuder (1982) The complexity of some polynomial network consistency algorithms (UBC TR 82-06)
finding: Time analysis of node, arc and path consistency. AC-3 is bounded above by O(a^3 e) and below by Omega(a^2 e), where a is domain size and e the number of binary constraints. Both are linear in e. Waltz filtering is a special case; on planar graphs the cost is linear in variables.
numbers: AC-3: O(a^3 e) upper, Omega(a^2 e) lower (2e original list length times a^2). PC-1 O(a^5 n^5); PC-2 O(a^5 n^3), an n^2 gain. Sparse graphs: AC-3 between a^2 n and a^3 n.
limits: O(a^3 e) was tightened to O(e a^2) by Zhang and Yap (a09). Worst case only.
agent_relevance: Arc consistency is cheap (linear in constraints); path consistency is not. Use arc-level checks always, path-level only on small cores.

source: Mackworth and Freuder (1982) Backtracking cost and trees
finding: Worst case for depth-first backtracking is O(e a^n): a^n leaves times e checks. So shrinking a before search matters most. If the constraint graph is a tree, node plus arc consistency lets a solution be built in at most O(a n) predicate evaluations, replacing an exponential algorithm with a linear one.
numbers: Tree: AC-3 in O(a^3 n), then O(a n) evaluations to instantiate. Backtracking O(e a^n).
limits: Tree result needs a binary, tree-shaped constraint graph.
agent_relevance: Test the problem graph for tree shape: if tree, propagation alone solves it with no search. This is a code-checkable branch.

source: Seidel (1983) On the complexity of achieving k-consistency (Cornell TR 83-04)
finding: Shows Freuder's k-consistency algorithm takes worst case time O(n^k) for n variables, with domain size constant. Repeats that Mackworth and Freuder settled the AC-3 question as linear in the number of constraints.
numbers: O(n^k) worst case.
limits: Worst case; constant domain size assumed.
agent_relevance: Higher-order consistency cost grows fast with order. Keep propagation at arc level and let search do the rest.

source: Freuder (1982) sufficient condition for backtrack-free search, as restated in van Beek (1994)
finding: Freuder (1978, 1982) generalised node, arc and path consistency to strong k-consistency. His 1982 theorem: an ordering of the variables in a binary network is backtrack-free if the level of strong k-consistency is greater than the width of the ordering. A tree has width 1, so arc consistency (k=2) is enough. The original JACM paper could not be opened; this is a secondary restatement.
numbers: Theorem 2 (Freuder 1982): strong k-consistency level > width of ordering gives backtrack-free search. Enforcing k-consistency costs O(n^k).
limits: Secondary source for Freuder; his own text was not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule the program can compute: find a variable order with low width, then lower-order consistency suffices. Order the sub-questions.

source: van Beek (1994) On the inherent level of local consistency in constraint networks
finding: New property, constraint looseness. If domains have size d or less and every constraint has looseness m or more (each value has at least m allowed partners), the network is strongly ceil(d/(d-m))-consistent. Loose constraints make low-order consistency useless as preprocessing. Random tests show loose networks can still be hard.
numbers: Strong ceil(d/(d-m))-consistency. Random tests: n=50 variables, |D| 5 to 10, constraint density p and tightness q each varied 1 to 100 percent; time to first solution measured. Example: n=5, |D|=5, 4-loose constraints give a globally consistent network.
limits: Bound is exact for some networks (graph k-colouring), loose for others. Binary constraints only.
agent_relevance: Tells the program when propagation will do nothing: if constraints are loose, skip it and go to search or sampling.

source: Zhang and Yap (2001) Making AC-3 an optimal algorithm
finding: AC-3, thought non-optimal since the O(e d^3) bound of Mackworth and Freuder (1985), is shown to run in worst case O(e d^2) by remembering the last support found for each value. Experiments: comparable to old AC-3 on easy problems, significantly faster on phase-transition hard problems, comparable to AC-6. Also shows the 24-year gap between the first estimate and the right bound.
numbers: Time O(e d^2), space O(e d), same as AC-6. Checks on hard instances: old AC-3.0 2,272,234 and 3,428,680 vs AC-3.1 787,151 and 999,708 vs AC-6 635,671 and 744,929 in two instance sets.
limits: 'Preliminary experiments' by the authors' own words; random and RLFAP instances only.
agent_relevance: Simple propagation plus a memory of why a value is still allowed is near-optimal. Cache supports in the agent's constraint log.

source: Mackworth, Mulder and Havens (1985) Hierarchical arc consistency
finding: When domain values group into a tree of subsets, hierarchical arc consistency (HAC) prunes whole groups at once. Best-case condition stated as O(log a (e+jn)) against AC-3's O(a^3 e); worst case remains O(a^3 e). On 10 sketch maps (Mapsee3, domains of 2 to 8 values) HAC used fewer predicate evaluations than AC-3 by factors up to about two.
numbers: Up to about 2x fewer evaluations on 10 maps; domain size a from 2 to 8.
limits: Gain needs hierarchical domain structure; small domains give small gain.
agent_relevance: Group answer options into classes and prune a class together. Fits O4 for large option sets.

source: Ginsberg (1993) Dynamic backtracking
finding: Chronological backtracking throws away good work in unrelated regions when it jumps back. Dynamic backtracking moves the backtrack point deeper, keeps independent progress, uses polynomial space and stays complete. Tested on crossword generation with iterative broadening, cheapest-first (most constrained) and forward checking.
numbers: 19 crossword frames, 2x2 to 13x13, 100 attempts each, limit 1000 backtracks. Dynamic backtracking more successful in 6 frames, less in none. Successes out of 100, dynamic vs backjumping: frame 15 99 vs 14, frame 16 100 vs 26, frame 18 61 vs 0, frame 19 10 vs 0.
limits: Author reports cases where it is worse (a region that is easy to recolour but is kept). One domain.
agent_relevance: When one part of a plan fails, keep the independent parts and revise only the culprit set. Supports G2.

source: Grant (1997) thesis, summary of Cheeseman et al. (1991) and Mitchell et al. (1992)
finding: Cheeseman, Kanefsky and Taylor (1991) found a phase transition in graph colouring: a region where almost all problems have many solutions and are easy, a region where almost all have none and insolubility is easy to prove, and a hard region between where the chance of a solution falls from near 1 to near 0 and mean search cost peaks. Mitchell, Selman and Levesque (1992) showed for SAT that the cost peak sits where 50 percent of instances are soluble. Reported here second-hand.
numbers: Cost peak where about 50 percent of sampled problems are soluble (SAT, Mitchell et al. 1992; binary CSP, Prosser 1996).
limits: Second-hand summary; the 1991 and 1992 papers were not opened. Random ensembles only.
agent_relevance: Difficulty depends on how constrained a task is, not on its size. The program can estimate constrainedness and route: loose, guess; critical, search hard; over-constrained, look for the contradiction.

source: Grant (1997) thesis, Smith and Dyer expected solutions and critical tightness
finding: For random binary CSPs with n variables, domain size m, density p1 and tightness p2, the expected number of solutions is E(N)=m^n (1-p2)^(p1 n(n-1)/2). Setting E(N)=1 predicts the crossover p2crit = 1 - m^(-2/(p1(n-1))). Prosser (1996) found this accurate except for sparse graphs, where it overestimates.
limits: Inaccurate for low p1; Model B random problems only.
agent_relevance: A code-computable difficulty estimate: expected solutions from sizes and tightness before spending budget.

source: Grant (1997) thesis ch. 6: phase transition of arc and path consistency (Grant and Smith 1996)
finding: Establishing arc consistency, a polynomial task, also shows an easy-hard-easy pattern. The cost peak sits where about 50 percent of problems can be made arc consistent. Arc consistency removes values mainly in the over-constrained region and does nothing in loose problems. AC3 average cost is close to linear in domain size m, far below worst case. Path consistency (PC2) is too costly as preprocessing.
numbers: Class <20,10,p1>, p1 0.2 to 1.0 step 0.1, p2 0.01 to 1.00 step 0.01, 1,000 problems per point. Cost about linear in m for already-consistent problems, between quadratic and cubic in m at the peak. Later Gent et al. (1997) predict cubic at the peak.
limits: Random binary Model B problems; structured problems untested.
agent_relevance: Propagation pays only where constraints are tight. Check first whether it removes anything; if not, stop doing it.

source: Grant (1997) thesis ch. 7: MAC versus forward checking (Grant and Smith 1996)
finding: Maintaining arc consistency (MAC) builds a far smaller search tree than forward checking (FC), stays backtrack-free over a wider range, and greatly reduces exceptionally hard problems. FC is cheaper in checks on small problems; MAC scales better as variables grow. Conflict-directed backjumping on top helps only the hardest searches. No champion algorithm exists.
numbers: Node and check counts over many binary CSP classes; FC check cost grows faster than MAC's on hard transition problems as n rises. No single ratio quoted in the text I read.
limits: Checks are implementation dependent; random CSPs; fail-first ordering used throughout.
agent_relevance: Stronger lookahead costs more per step but wins on hard tasks. Choose propagation depth by estimated difficulty.

source: Grant (1997) thesis ch. 5: exceptionally hard problems
finding: Some very costly searches occur where most problems are easy. Cause: thrashing on an insoluble sub-problem that plain backtracking cannot see, when an early choice leaves a later variable with an empty domain. Forward checking and look-ahead largely remove it. Same pattern as a SAT instance needing over 350 million branches (Gent and Walsh 1994).
numbers: Gent and Walsh 1994 SAT case: more than 350 million branches. Hogg and Williams found a second cost peak in high percentiles before the phase transition.
limits: Behaviour of one algorithm, not a truly hard instance; Model B random problems.
agent_relevance: Heavy tails: the mean hides disasters. Cap per-branch effort, restart, and check the future domain after each choice (an empty one means stop now).

source: Grant (1997) thesis ch. 8: the fail-first principle (Smith and Grant 1997)
finding: Haralick and Elliott's fail-first (pick the variable with the smallest domain) works, but its explanation, maximise the chance of failure, is not supported: heuristics built on more accurate fail-probability estimates did not do better. Heuristics using global degree beat those using subproblem degree, against the principle. DD (domain over degree) did extremely well except on fully connected graphs.
numbers: Tested on FC and MAC over many classes of (n,m,p1,p2) CSPs; predicted ordering of heuristics not borne out. Matches Hooker and Vinay (1995) on SAT branching.
limits: Random binary CSPs; explanation offered only tentatively.
agent_relevance: Use smallest-domain-first as a rule of thumb for what to resolve next. Do not trust fancier failure prediction; test on held-out tasks (G7).

source: Xu and Li (2000) Exact phase transitions in random CSPs (Model RB)
finding: Proposes Model RB, a revision of Model B, and proves a phase transition as variables grow, with exact critical values; instances at the threshold are hard. Only the abstract page was readable; the PDF text was garbled.
numbers: Not recorded; abstract only. From memory the threshold is p_cr = 1 - e^(-alpha/r); not verified.
limits: Abstract only. Motive: standard Model B becomes trivially easy at scale.
agent_relevance: A source of hard random test problems for benchmarking the scaffold's constraint tools.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: scaling limits of LLMs for logical reasoning (ICML)
finding: Logic grid puzzles as CSPs, 1,000 puzzles, N houses by M attributes, search space (N!)^M, plus Z3 conflict count as a second difficulty measure. Accuracy collapses as complexity rises (the 'curse of complexity'); scaling model size helps little.
numbers: Overall grid accuracy: o1-full 81.0, DeepSeek-R1 78.7, o1-preview 71.4, o1-mini 59.7, Sonnet-3.5 36.2, Llama-3.1-405B 32.6, GPT-4o 31.7. X-Large (over 10^10): o1-full 42.5, R1 28.5, o1-preview 17.0, GPT-4o 0.5, 405B 0.0.
limits: Greedy decoding for non-o1 models; o1 best of three runs; one puzzle family; X-Large columns read from a garbled table so check before quoting.
agent_relevance: Models fail where propagation plus search is needed. Offloading constraint bookkeeping to code is the clear opening for O4/S4.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, test-time compute
finding: More samples help only a little with practical selection. GPT-4o: best-of-32 with an oracle 60.3, oracle best-of-128 69.1, but majority vote only 38.0 (N=32) and 37.6 (N=128) from a 31.7 base; reward-model selection 34.8. Self-verify prompts gave marginal gains. o1 models write about 5,100 to 5,300 hidden reasoning tokens vs about 500 for GPT-4o and scale with Z3 conflicts, roughly 400 tokens per conflict under 20 conflicts, plateauing above 30.
numbers: GPT-4o 31.7; majority N=32 38.0; oracle N=32 60.3; BoN-RM N=32 34.8; hidden tokens o1-mini 5,144.6, o1-preview 5,346.3, GPT-4o-mini 502.9, GPT-4o 543.7.
limits: Oracle selection is not available in practice. Hidden token counts are estimates.
agent_relevance: Independent samples do not fix CSPs (matches G4, G5). Success needs real backtracking: a program that tracks domains and conflicts, not more votes.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, CSP formulation and Z3 conflicts
finding: Variables x(a,k) for attribute a in house k, with uniqueness constraints plus clues. Puzzles with zero Z3 conflicts are solvable by forward chaining alone; more conflicts need backtracking. Most models struggle once the search space exceeds 10^7 (e.g. a 4x5 grid) or conflicts exceed 20.
numbers: Z3 run 32 times per puzzle, mean conflicts as complexity. Groups: Small under 10^3, Medium 10^3 to 10^6, Large 10^6 to 10^10, X-Large over 10^10.
limits: Conflict count depends on solver and encoding.
agent_relevance: A cheap difficulty signal: run a solver for conflicts. Zero conflicts means propagation is enough and no search is needed.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LR2Bench: long-chain reflective reasoning via CSPs
finding: 850 samples over six CSPs (Crossword, Acrostic, Logic Puzzle, Cryptogram, Sudoku, Drop Quote). Even top reasoning models score low on exact match (EM).
numbers: Mean EM: DeepSeek-R1 20.0, o1-preview 23.6, o1-mini 9.1. Sudoku EM: o1-preview 50.0, Mistral-Large 50.0, o1-mini 27.0, GPT-4o 14.5. Cryptogram EM: o1-preview 13.0, R1 4.0, GPT-4o 0.0. Logic Puzzle EM: o1-preview 41.0.
limits: Few models; mean tokens up to about 14,000, so some failures are length, not logic.
agent_relevance: Models fill many cells (high partial scores) but miss the fully consistent assignment. Code that checks all constraints closes this gap.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LR2Bench, redundancy and missing reflection
finding: Reasoning models often repeat themselves on contradictions until the length limit; 10-gram redundancy correlates strongly and negatively with completion rate. Conventional models do not cross-check clues against each other, giving high partial accuracy but near-zero EM on Crossword and Acrostic. The gap to reasoning models is largest on Logic Puzzle and Sudoku (o1-preview over GPT-4o: +37.5 and +35.5 EM).
numbers: EM gain o1-preview over GPT-4o: Logic Puzzle +37.5, Sudoku +35.5; QwQ-32B-Preview over Qwen2.5-72B: +19.5 and +26.0.
limits: Correlation, not causation, for redundancy.
agent_relevance: Contradictions trigger loops. A program-side loop and conflict detector (G1) would cut the waste.

source: Bonlarron, Regin, De Maria and Regin (2025) LLM meets constraint propagation (GenCP with masked LMs)
finding: GenCP casts text generation as a CSP: variables are words or tokens, domains come from LLM top-k or top-p predictions, a CP solver enforces constraints with backtracking. Adding a masked language model (BERT) to preview future-token domains gives bidirectional propagation and fewer LLM calls on COLLIE tasks.
numbers: sent-1: vanilla 444 LLM calls, 375 backtracks, 3 solutions; meta-variables 456 calls, 211 backtracks, 4; MLM preview (depth 2, 32 MLM calls) 359 calls, 170 backtracks, 10. para-2: metavar 446 calls, 136 backtracks, 3 solutions; preview 341 calls, 40 MLM calls, 193 backtracks, 6. para-4: metavar 466 calls, 447 backtracks, 0 solutions; preview 422 calls, 258 backtracks, 2.
limits: Small models (babbage-002, bert-base-cased); few runs; preview sometimes raises backtracks.
agent_relevance: Closest direct example: the LLM proposes domain values, a solver propagates and backtracks. This is the O4/S4 design with code in control.

source: Bonlarron et al. (2025) GenCP: limits and backtracking
finding: Without meta-variables GenCP searches only very short frequent tokens (as, they, their, a). Limited backtracking can find constrained text that greedy generation misses, while complete backtracking can push the LLM into low-likelihood regions. MLMs are trained on about 15 percent masked tokens, which limits preview depth; deeper previews gave fewer solutions in equal time.
numbers: MLM trained on about 15 percent masked tokens; preview depth 2 gave gains, deeper gave fewer solutions per unit time.
limits: Authors' own caveats; one benchmark family.
agent_relevance: Bound backtracking by model likelihood: restart or fall back to best-so-far when likelihood drops below a threshold (G6).

source: Zhang and Yap (2001) history of AC-3 bounds
finding: Controversy over AC-3 cost: Mackworth (1977) first estimates; Mackworth and Freuder (1982, 1985) settle O(e a^3); Zhang and Yap (2001) tighten to O(e d^2). Textbook complexity claims can be loose for decades; measured averages sit far below worst case (Wallace 1993, Grant 1997).
numbers: Bounds in order: O(a^2) in arcs (1977), O(a^3 e) (1982/85), O(e d^2) (2001).
limits: Worst case differs widely from average case.
agent_relevance: Distrust worst-case estimates. Measure cost on the agent's own tasks.
